You use the Future Perfect tense to talk about something that will be complete by a certain time in the future.

When you use the Future Perfect, you often refer to a time period (next month, tomorrow, this afternoon, by Friday).
For example:
Do you think you will have completed the report by Friday?
You often use the preposition by with the Future Perfect. By means no later than or can suggest the idea of progress up to a particular time.
Look at the chart for the form of the Future Perfect:

Intonation of Finished and Unfinished Ideas
Intonation tells us a lot about how someone feels and whether they have completed their thoughts or not. It is important to listen carefully to the rise and fall of people's voices.
Being able to listen for intonation is especially important when you are speaking on the phone.
In English, there are three intonation patterns:

You should use falling intonation at the end of a thought group or sentence to tell the listener that you are finished with that statement.
For example:
Under the circumstances, that doesn't appear necessary. ⤵

Likewise, your pitch will only partially fall at the end of a thought group to:
give the listener's brain time to “digest” the speech; and
tell the listener that you are not finished speaking.

For example:
I was going to comb my hair … ➖➖
Let's see…  Oh yes, I wrote an article about what people thought the new student center should be called. I suggested the name Humpty Dumpty Place.
Ohhh.... Did you say Humpty Dumpty Place?
Ummm…. yes, I guess so. I was going to comb my hair …
This is Julia Allen calling from Never Odd Or Even.
That seems to be a logical choice.

You use rising intonation at the end of a yes/no question.
For example:
Did you say Humpty Dumpty Place? ⤴

images.text:
Ms. Allen: Hello, is this Adam Bari?
Adam: Yes it is.
Ms. Allen: Hello, Adam. This is Julia Allen calling from Never Odd Or Even.
Adam: Oh yes, I'm leaving for my interview shortly. Is there a problem?
Ms. Allen: No, Mr. Bari. You will have to start with a phone interview. If that goes well, we will invite you to our offices to meet the director in person.
Adam: Oh, but I just bought a great tie.
Ms. Allen: Well, I'm sure you'll have the opportunity to wear it to the second interview. Are you ready for the phone interview, Mr. Bari?
Adam: Ummm ... yes, I guess so. I was going to comb my hair ...

Ms. Allen: Under the circumstances, that doesn't appear necessary. Could you describe your professional experiences for me please?
Adam: Sure. Most of my experience comes from working on the campus newspaper. Next month, I will have volunteered there for over two years.
Ms. Allen: Could you tell me what you do there?
Adam: With pleasure. Over the past two years, I have performed a variety of tasks. I was a copy editor and proofreader, and I wrote an editorial once a month. Now, I sell advertising space to local businesses.
Ms. Allen: As web content editor, you will help us think of interesting ideas for stories. Could you tell me about the issues you covered?
Adam: I'd love to. I wrote a lot of editorials related to student life at the college.

Ms. Allen: Could you give me some examples?
Adam: Absolutely. Let's see … Oh yes, I wrote an article about what people thought the new student center should be called. I suggested the name Humpty Dumpty Place.
Ms. Allen: Ohhh ... Did you say Humpty Dumpty Place?
Adam: Yes, I thought it was funny at the time, but they chose the name Thomas Dudley Pavillion instead. He was the founder of Cambridge.
Ms. Allen: That seems to be a logical choice.
Adam: I suppose so. Logic hasn't always been my forte.
